results.title: Pass/Fail Criteria for IP Wet Testing
results.content: 1 www.CertifiGroup.com Experts in UL, CSA, CE & International Regulatory Compliance © 2007 - 2018 CertifiGroup - complete copies of this document may be freely distributed 8-5-18 Pass/Fail Criteria for IP Wet Testing Ingress Protection Testing IP Wet Testing: Ingress Protection (IP) testing determines a product’s protection level against ingress of solid objects and/or water. Pass/Fail Criteria: The acceptance conditions for IP wet tests per IEC 60529 states that it is the responsibility of the relevant technical committee (end product standard) to determine the unacceptable amount of water that may enter the product. Product functionality is not the only pass/fail criteria for IP wet testing. Every product that is IP wet tested must be immediately disassembled and visually inspected for water deposits on all electrical parts and in critical safety areas.

results.title: Integrating Prompt Optimization With Safety Protocols To Build Trustworthy AI — Especially When Stakes Are High | by Jyoti Shah | Medium
results.content: # Integrating Prompt Optimization With Safety Protocols To Build Trustworthy AI — Especially When Stakes Are High. Marrying prompt optimization with your existing safety protocols can measurably reduce harm, hallucinations, and operational risk [1]–[3]. In these contexts, trust comes from process, not promises — specifically, from integrating prompt optimization techniques with the safety controls your organization already uses [1], [2], [5]. Before wordsmithing your prompts, classify use cases by risk (e.g., **informational**, **operational**, **regulatory**, **safety-critical**). When auditors ask “what told the model to do X?”, you should be able to point to a specific prompt version and diff [1], [2]. **Prompt technique:** *Policy-grounded role prompting.* Assign the model a role aligned to governance (e.g., *“You are a compliance-aware assistant that must follow the approved decision tree and refuse outside scope”*). • Require **JSON or schema-validated formats** (e.g., fields for confidence, citations, risk flags, action type). • *Constitutional/criteria prompts* for the checker (evaluate against explicit safety criteria; return pass/fail + reasons) [7]. • *Adversarial self-queries* (“List reasons this response might violate policy; if any, refuse.”), which align with red-team findings in modern system cards [6], [14]. • *Source-attribution prompting* (require an evidence field per claim), improving auditability against frameworks like NIST AI RMF and ISO guidance [1], [3]. • Track **prompt robustness metrics**: policy-violation rate, harmful content rate, jailbreak susceptibility, refusal precision/recall, abstention accuracy. • *Few-shot “hard cases”* embedded in the system prompt to set strict refusal behavior [7]. Tie these SLOs to automated **circuit breakers**: if violation rates spike, degrade capability (e.g., read-only mode), tighten prompts, or require human approval until stability returns. Provide one-click **rollback to a safe prompt version** and a playbook for incident response: isolate, reproduce, patch prompt/rules, re-test, and release with a changelog [1], [2]. • **System prompt:** Encodes clinical scope, mandatory refusals (no diagnosis), and escalation triggers (e.g., chest pain → “call emergency services”). • **Structured output:** `{ disposition, risk_factors[], evidence[], can_act, escalation_reason }`, validated before display/action [3], [4]. • **Safety sandwich:** Generator proposes a disposition; checker verifies guideline alignment and refuses if evidence is weak [7]. • **Pretty but brittle prompts:** Over-optimized wording that collapses under edge cases.

results.title: Release Metadata - Ryvn
results.content: * **Track exact artifacts** used in each release (container images, Helm charts, etc.) * **Manage service dependencies** and ensure proper deployment order * **Compute valid migration paths** between versions * **Enable automated rollbacks** with confidence Release artifacts define the exact artifacts (like container images) that are part of a release. ### ​ Each release specifies a list of supported schema versions: * **Current schema versions**: The schema versions that this release supports * **Migration path validation**: Ryvn ensures rollbacks only target supported schema versions * **Version compatibility**: Prevents deployment to releases with incompatible schemas ### ​ repository: ghcr.io/my-org/my-app - version: 4 # Schema version 4 is supported - version: 5 # Schema version 5 is supported - version: 6 # Schema version 6 is supported ### ​ Ryvn uses the supported schema versions to: 1. Ryvn analyzes the supported schema versions of both current and target releases Validates that the target release supports the current schema version Ensures rollback targets only supported schema versions Allows or blocks deployment based on schema compatibility ### ​ You can include custom metadata for your specific use cases: repository: ghcr.io/my-org/my-app - version: 4 # Schema version 4 is supported - version: 5 # Schema version 5 is supported - version: 6 # Schema version 6 is supported releaseNotes: "Added new user authentication features" ### ​ Ryvn validates release metadata to ensure: * **Artifact consistency**: Artifacts match the service type * **Dependency validity**: Referenced services exist and are accessible * **Migration compatibility**: Migration scripts are valid SQL * **Version compatibility**: Dependencies are compatible with the release version ### ​ Release metadata can inherit from previous releases: repository: ghcr.io/my-org/my-app ### ​ Use semantic versioning for all artifacts Include checksums for artifact integrity Tag artifacts with the same version as the release ### ​ Keep dependencies minimal and well-defined Use version ranges for flexible dependency resolution Document breaking changes in dependencies ### ​ Test migrations in staging environments first Include rollback scripts for all migrations Use database transactions for atomic migrations ### ​ Keep metadata up-to-date with each release Validate metadata before creating releases Review and clean up old metadata periodically ### ​ Ensure the artifact repository and tag are accessible from Ryvn’s infrastructure.

results.content: # Understanding Pass/Fail Criteria for an ASTM E119 Fire Test. We rely on the ASTM E119 testing method. ## **What Is an ASTM E119 Fire Test?**. The ASTM E119 fire test is a standardized test method used to evaluate the fire resistance of building components and assemblies. The results of an ASTM E119 fire test provide valuable information for building code officials, architects, engineers, and construction professionals. The test helps ensure that building components and assemblies meet the required fire safety standards and provide a level of protection to occupants and property in the event of a fire. ## **How We Conduct an ASTM E119 Fire Test**. In the ASTM E119 fire test, the evaluation of a building component's fire resistance is determined based on pass/fail criteria. The following critical, timed events are recorded during the ASTM E119 test. In many cases, the ASTM E119 test requires an additional evaluation of the assembly, where it is subjected to a hose stream test to establish a fire-resistance rating. It's important to note that the specific pass/fail criteria may vary depending on the fire rating being tested and the applicable building codes and regulations. Building code officials, architects, and engineers rely on the results of an ASTM E119 fire test to verify compliance with fire safety standards and make informed decisions regarding the design and construction of fire-resistant buildings. ### **What types of products can be tested using ASTM E119?**. ### **What is considered a “pass” for ASTM E119 testing?**. If a component fails any of the criteria during the test, it cannot receive the desired fire-resistance rating. ### **Is NGC Testing Services accredited for ASTM E119?**. Yes. NGC Testing Services is fully accredited and has decades of experience conducting ASTM E119 tests for commercial, industrial, and residential products.
